design_detail: Inpatient human laboratory study on a residential research unit (about 6 weeks per participant; Johns Hopkins IRB) comparing two groups of 8 adults not seeking treatment who smoked or injected cocaine: DSM-IV cocaine abuse without dependence (CocAb; cocaine on average no more than twice a week) and DSM-IV cocaine dependence (CocDep; 6 or more days a week), matched on years of cocaine use, then sex, age and race (Table 1 shows similar distributions rather than exact pairs). Within each person, double-blind, placebo-controlled intravenous cocaine: one dose-response session (0, 12.5, 25 and 50 mg/70 kg given 1 h apart in fixed ascending order); six sample sessions (one dose of 0, 12.5 or 25 mg/70 kg), each followed the next day by a self-administration session, three with a Relapse Choice Procedure (seven choices between the sampled dose and money falling from $19 to $1) and three with a Progressive Ratio Procedure (up to seven doses for 50 to 2500 button presses); order of procedures counterbalanced and order of doses randomized within each procedure. Trait questionnaires and the Iowa gambling task were given once, before any dose. The dose comparisons are within person; the comparison between diagnostic groups is observational (diagnosis was not assigned).
can_establish: Within these 16 people, how intravenous cocaine at 12.5 to 50 mg/70 kg compared with saline changed subjective ratings, heart rate, blood pressure and pupil size, how often they chose cocaine over money or worked for it, and whether the 8 meeting dependence criteria differed from the 8 meeting abuse criteria on these measures and on trait questionnaires at one point in time.
cannot_establish: Why dependence develops in some people and not others: the groups were selected by current frequency of use (5 vs 28.5 days in the past 30), so any difference may reflect current exposure, tolerance or recent use rather than a characteristic that preceded dependence, and nothing was measured before regular use began; equivalence on impulsivity or sensation seeking (with 8 per group only differences of about 1.5 standard deviations had 80% power); effects of the smoked route that 15 of the 16 preferred, since all laboratory doses were intravenous.

sample.recruitment: Advertisement: local newspaper advertisements and word of mouth; healthy adult volunteers not seeking treatment, living as inpatients on a residential research unit for about 6 weeks and paid $24 per night (p. 29, 2.1 and 2.2). Of 190 who completed an initial in-person assessment, 132 were disqualified before the second intake (medical reasons 51, drug-use frequency 39, inadequate venous access 13, not interested 11, insufficient literacy 10, other 8); 58 had the SCID interview, of whom 32 were disqualified (substance-use diagnosis 14, other psychiatric diagnosis 9, other 9); 26 were enrolled (14%), 19 completed and 16 matched completers are reported (Table 1 and 3.1.1, p. 31; 3.1.3, p. 32).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All: at least 6 months of cocaine use, use within the past 30 days, smoking or injecting route; good health on history, examination, ECG and laboratory tests; no psychiatric disorder other than drug use disorders on the SCID. Excluded: seeking treatment, history of seizures, cardiovascular disease or diabetes, pregnancy, physical dependence on any drug other than nicotine and caffeine. CocAb: cocaine on average no more than twice weekly for the 2 months before admission, DSM-IV cocaine abuse but not dependence. CocDep: cocaine on average 6 or more days a week for the 2 months before admission, DSM-IV cocaine dependence including at least one of the two loss-of-control criteria (p. 29, 2.1, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: CocAb: 6 men, 2 women; 5 White, 3 African American; age 37.6 (SD 6.61); education 11 years (SD 1.51); cocaine on 5.25 of the past 30 days (SD 3.28, range 1 to 10); 14.38 years since first use (SD 7.03, range 2 to 23). CocDep: 5 men, 3 women; 4 White, 3 African American, 1 Hispanic; age 35.1 (SD 4.88); education 12.25 years (SD 1.75); cocaine on 28.5 of the past 30 days (SD 3.51, range 20 to 30); 14.13 years since first use (SD 6.33, range 5 to 23) (Table 1, p. 31; the plus-or-minus values are sample SDs, editors' recalculation from the individual rows). All preferred smoking except one CocDep participant who preferred injection; other drugs (alcohol, heroin, benzodiazepines, cannabis) on 6 or fewer occasions in the past 30 days in both groups (p. 32, 3.1.3, 2nd paragraph).
sample.attrition: Of 26 enrolled, 7 left early: 4 for non-medical reasons, 1 after learning of a positive HIV test, 2 for exceeding blood-pressure safety criteria during testing (p. 31, 3.1.1). Of 19 completers, 3 could not be matched and are not reported; their diagnostic group is not stated (p. 32, 3.1.3).
sample.selection_effects: Highly selected: 16 analysed of 190 assessed. The groups were defined in part by current frequency of use (an a priori criterion; days of use in the past 30, t[14] = 13.69), so diagnosis and current exposure are confounded by design. People seeking treatment, with psychiatric comorbidity, other drug dependence, cardiovascular disease or poor venous access were excluded, and two who exceeded blood-pressure limits were discharged, which selects people who tolerate intravenous cocaine. Matching appears to be at group level (similar, not identical, sex and race mix) and unmatched completers were dropped. Six weeks of residence and payment select people able to live on a research unit.

exposure.measurement: Diagnosis by the SCID (DSM-IV), given by trained master's-level psychometricians and reviewed by a supervisor; history and days of cocaine use by self-report (p. 29, 2.1; Table 1, p. 31). Laboratory exposure: pharmaceutical cocaine hydrochloride in sterile saline or saline placebo, infused intravenously by a physician over 60 s (p. 30, 2.5).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, all intravenous: dose-response session 0, 12.5, 25 and 50 mg/70 kg, 1 h apart in ascending order; sample sessions one dose of 0, 12.5 or 25 mg/70 kg; self-administration sessions up to seven doses of the sampled dose at least 15 min apart. A planned 50 mg/70 kg self-administration condition was removed by protocol amendment after doses were delayed or withheld for cardiovascular readings, and its data were excluded (p. 30, 2.3.2 to 2.3.5; p. 31, 3.1.2).
exposure.polysubstance: Dependence on drugs other than nicotine and caffeine excluded. Other drug use in the past 30 days described only as 6 or fewer occasions of alcohol, heroin, benzodiazepines and cannabis in both groups, without figures by group (p. 32). Tobacco smoking was allowed on the unit except 1.5 h before and during sessions and was not quantified; caffeine was not allowed (p. 29, 2.2).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Inpatients on a residential research unit for about 6 weeks; the assessment session took place at least 3 days after admission (p. 29, 2.2). Urine testing before sessions, any cocaine use outside the laboratory sessions and withdrawal measures are not reported.

comparison.controls: Within person: saline placebo (0 mg) in every procedure. Between groups: 8 CocAb against 8 CocDep; no group without cocaine use.
comparison.matching: Matched first on years of cocaine use, then on sex, age and race (p. 32, 3.1.3); Table 1 shows similar group distributions (6 vs 5 men; 5 vs 4 White) rather than exact pairs, so matching appears to be at group level. Education not matched (11 vs 12.25 years, not significantly different).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measure from before regular cocaine use; impulsivity and sensation seeking were measured only at study entry, after about 14 years of use; age at first use and years of use are recalled.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Both groups reported low use of other drugs; the abuse group itself used cocaine on 1 to 10 days a month.

outcomes.instruments: Trait (once, before any dose): NEO personality inventory, Eysenck Impulsivity Scale (I-7), Zuckerman Sensation Seeking Scale, Barratt Impulsiveness Scale, Iowa gambling task (100 cards). After doses: six 100-point visual analogue items (any drug effect, rush, good effects, bad effects, liking, desire for cocaine), a street-value estimate, a 22-item subject-rated and a 9-item observer-rated adjective checklist (0 to 4); heart rate, blood pressure and skin temperature each minute, respiration, pupil diameter; Multiple-Choice Procedure crossover value; number of cocaine choices and money earned (Relapse Choice); ratios completed (Progressive Ratio) (pp. 29-30, 2.3 and 2.4).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard questionnaires; the authors state that mean trait scores were comparable to earlier samples of people with cocaine dependence (p. 36). No group without cocaine use and no normative comparison.
outcomes.operationalization: Unpleasant effects: main effects of group on subject-rated suspicious and observer-rated moody, difficulty concentrating, fidgety, drug effect and edgy or irritable, from time-course data of the dose-response session (baseline excluded from the dose analysis, not adjusted for) or peak values (pp. 30-33). Desire: the visual analogue item. Taking more cocaine: injections chosen out of seven, money forgone, ratios completed, crossover value.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: every test at p of 0.05 or less, with Tukey post hoc tests within ANOVAs (p. 31). Editors' count of outcomes compared between groups: 14 trait subscales, the gambling task, 6 analogue items, 31 adjective items, street value, 6 physiological measures, the crossover value and 3 self-administration measures; about a dozen are reported as differing.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants and the staff who ran sessions and collected data (including observer ratings) were blind to dose and to diagnostic group (p. 29, 2.2). In the dose-response session doses rose in a fixed order, which limits blinding to dose there; blinding was not checked.

analysis.effect_sizes: All comparisons 8 vs 8. Baseline before any dose: desire for cocaine higher in CocDep, t[14] = 2.43, p = 0.045; observer-rated edgy or irritable lower in CocDep, t(14) = -2.65, p = 0.033 (p. 32, 3.2.1). Desire across the dose-response session: group F(1,14) = 6.7, p = 0.022; group by time F(12,168) = 2.3, p = 0.009 (Fig. 1, p. 32). Adjective checklist, main effects of group: suspicious F = 7.9 (higher CocAb), crave cocaine F = 6.0 and sweating F = 7.1 (higher CocDep), observer-rated moody F(1,14) = 4.98, p = 0.043, difficulty concentrating F = 5.9, p = 0.029, fidgety F = 5.21, p = 0.039, drug effect F(1,14) = 4.7 and edgy or irritable F = 12.2 (higher CocAb) (p. 33; Fig. 2). Street value: group by dose F(3,42) = 5.1, p = 0.005; at 50 mg/70 kg $10.88 (CocAb) vs $30.38 (CocDep) (p. 33). Relapse Choice: injections chosen, group F(1,14) = 5.27, p = 0.038, dose F(2,28) = 3.4, p = 0.049; money earned, dose F(2,28) = 3.69, p = 0.038, group p = 0.055 (p. 33; Fig. 3, p. 34). Progressive Ratio: dose F(2,28) = 8.43, p = 0.001; group F(1,14) = 3.92, printed p = 0.056 (p. 33; Fig. 4). Multiple-Choice crossover: dose F(2,28) = 6.3, p = 0.006; group F(1,14) = 4.9, p = 0.044 (Fig. 5, p. 34). The two self-administration measures correlated, Spearman rho = 0.76, p < 0.001. No group differences on any drug effect, high, rush, good effects, liking, heart rate, blood pressure or pupil diameter, on any trait subscale, or on overall gambling-task choice. No confidence intervals or standardized effect sizes are reported. Editors' reading of the individual points in Figs 3 and 4 (whole numbers, 8 per group; bars agree to about 0.1): injections chosen out of seven, CocAb vs CocDep, 0 vs 1.6 at placebo, 1.5 vs 3.75 at 12.5 mg/70 kg, 2.75 vs about 5.4 at 25 mg/70 kg; ratios completed 0 vs 0.25, 2.0 vs about 4.9, 3.25 vs 6.0. Editors' calculation from Table 2 (mean and SEM, n = 8): standardized differences for the 14 trait subscales lie between -0.57 and +0.57, each with a 95% interval about 2 SD wide (Barratt d = 0.03, -0.96 to 1.01).
analysis.covariates: None. Mixed-design ANOVAs on raw time-course data (baseline excluded but not adjusted for) and on peaks; t-tests for baseline and demographic comparisons (pp. 30-31, 2.7).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned; the 50 mg/70 kg self-administration condition was dropped by protocol amendment for safety.
analysis.selective_reporting: Results for the self-rated bad-effects item, listed in the Methods (p. 30), are not reported, although the abstract concludes that the abuse group had more unpleasant effects; high is reported in the Results (p. 32) but is not among the items listed in the Methods. Subjective and physiological data from the self-administration sessions are not presented, because of varied patterns of administration (p. 33). Several group effects are given as an F value without df or p (suspicious, crave cocaine, sweating, edgy or irritable) and the gambling-task bin differences only as p < 0.05 (p. 35).
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors note that limited power may affect the trait comparisons (p. 36). Editors' calculation: with 8 per group, 80% power at two-sided p = 0.05 only for standardized differences of about 1.5 or more.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 16 inpatients chosen for daily vs at most twice-weekly cocaine use, intravenous cocaine produced dose-related increases in positive ratings, heart rate and blood pressure that did not differ by diagnosis. The dependence group reported more desire for cocaine before any dose and throughout, put a higher street value on the doses, chose active cocaine over money about twice as often at both active doses and had higher crossover values; the progressive-ratio difference was not significant. The abuse group scored higher on subject-rated suspiciousness and on a few observer-rated adverse items (main effects of group, without reported group by dose interactions). No differences on impulsivity, sensation seeking or overall gambling-task choice.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says that after cocaine the abuse group reported more suspiciousness and was rated higher on unpleasant effects, and the conclusion suggests this greater sensitivity to unpleasant effects may be a protective mechanism against escalation (p. 28; p. 36). The group differences are main effects, not group by dose interactions; the abuse group was already rated higher on edgy or irritable before any dose (p. 32), and its means are higher after placebo in Fig. 2 (p. 33), so the differences are not shown to be produced by cocaine; the self-rated bad-effects item is not reported. The authors themselves offer tolerance in the people using cocaine daily as an alternative (p. 35), and the groups were defined by frequency of use, so a protective trait cannot be told apart from current exposure. The conclusion that dependent individuals took all available cocaine in both the presence and absence of alternative reinforcers (p. 36) rests in its second half on a non-significant progressive-ratio difference (printed p = 0.056; the printed F gives about 0.068). The statement that laboratory self-administration was predicted by self-reported use before entry (p. 35) has no reported analysis beyond the group difference that defined the groups.

timeline.event: Higgins, Bickel and Hughes: an alternative reinforcer (money) reduced human cocaine self-administration; cited by the authors for the lower intake when money was available (p. 35); not appraised.

Mendelson et al.: one intravenous dose of 28 mg/70 kg in men using cocaine occasionally (5 to 10 occasions in the past year) produced larger cardiovascular, euphoria and ACTH responses than in men with cocaine dependence; as described by the authors, who note the exposure histories differed from this study (p. 35); not appraised.
Hart et al.: alternative reinforcers and cocaine self-administration in people (title of the reference record); to be appraised.
This study: first laboratory comparison of people with DSM-IV cocaine dependence and people with cocaine abuse who use regularly, by the authors' account (pp. 35-36).

replication.where_it_stands: A single small study without replication reported in the paper. Its within-person dose effects (positive ratings, heart rate, blood pressure) are expected and consistent; its comparison of diagnostic groups is confounded by current frequency of use and needs a design that separates diagnosis from current exposure.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse grants R0114653 (S.L. Walsh) and T320007209 (E.C. Donny); NIDA had no further role in study design, data collection, analysis and interpretation, writing or the decision to submit (p. 36, Role of funding source).
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors declare no conflicts of interest that could inappropriately influence, or be perceived to influence, the work (p. 36).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Kentucky Center on Drug and Alcohol Research, University of Pittsburgh, and the Johns Hopkins Behavioral Pharmacology Research Unit; approved by the Johns Hopkins Institutional Review Board (pp. 28-29).

what_would_settle_it: A larger laboratory study comparing people with and without a cocaine use disorder who are matched on current frequency and amount of use, with pre-registered outcomes, randomized dose order, reporting of all adverse-effect items and baseline-adjusted analyses; and, for the question of what leads to dependence, a prospective cohort that measures sensitivity to cocaine's unpleasant effects before regular use begins.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of doses and procedures)
domains.note: Dose order was randomized within each self-administration procedure and the order of procedures counterbalanced (method not described), but the dose-response session, the source of the subjective and cardiovascular dose effects, gave 0, 12.5, 25 and 50 mg/70 kg in a fixed ascending order, so dose is confounded with time and cumulative dose there.

Sessions were at least 24 h apart, but in the dose-response session each dose was given 1 h after the previous one, so later doses act on top of earlier ones; each self-administration session followed a sample dose the day before.

Double-blind to dose and diagnostic group, but blinding was not checked and active intravenous cocaine is recognizable to people who use it (the abuse group never chose placebo over money); doses were delayed or withheld for cardiovascular readings (6 delayed and 17 withheld among the first 9 participants, 8 delayed and 2 withheld later).
7 of 26 enrolled left early (2 for blood pressure), 3 completers were excluded by matching, and the 50 mg/70 kg self-administration data were excluded after the amendment.
Physiological and choice measures are objective; ratings by participants and observers are subjective and blinding may have been incomplete.
No registration; 63 outcomes without correction; the self-rated bad-effects item and the self-administration-session ratings are not reported; several statistics lack df or p values.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: RoB 2 is applied to the within-person comparisons of cocaine doses with placebo, the randomized part of the design. The dose-related increases in positive ratings, heart rate and blood pressure are large and consistent, but the fixed ascending order in the dose-response session and the unreported outcomes give a high risk of bias. The paper's main contrast, dependence against abuse, is between non-randomized groups and is outside RoB 2: judged as an observational comparison it would be at very high risk of bias with ROBINS-E, because the groups were selected on current frequency of use, there are 8 people per group, many outcomes and no adjustment, and the adverse-effect differences were present before any dose. Cite for: the dose-related subjective and cardiovascular effects of intravenous cocaine at 12.5 to 50 mg/70 kg in this laboratory setting; that people with daily use meeting dependence criteria chose cocaine over money more often in the laboratory than people using at most twice a week. Do not cite for: a trait that protects against dependence, a mechanism of the transition to dependence, or the absence of impulsivity differences.

key_findings.finding: 190 people completed an initial assessment, 26 (14%) were enrolled as inpatients, 19 completed the protocol and 16 matched completers (8 per group) are reported; 2 of the 7 who left early exceeded blood-pressure safety criteria.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (upper half) and Results › 3.1.1 Recruitment (p. 31); 3.1.3 Matching, 1st paragraph (p. 32)

key_findings.finding: The groups differed by design in current use: cocaine on 5.25 (SD 3.28) vs 28.5 (SD 3.51) of the past 30 days, t[14] = 13.69, p < 0.0001; they were similar in years since first use (14.38 vs 14.13), age (37.6 vs 35.1), education (11 vs 12.25 years) and sex (6 and 5 men of 8).
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (lower half), p. 31; Results › 3.1.3 Matching, 2nd paragraph, p. 32

key_findings.finding: During enrolment of the first 9 participants, 6 doses were delayed and 17 withheld because of raised cardiovascular readings; the 50 mg/70 kg self-administration condition was then removed and its data excluded; afterwards 8 doses were delayed and 2 withheld.

Intravenous cocaine produced dose- and time-related increases in ratings of any drug effect, high, rush, good effects and liking (p < 0.0001; rush, dose F(3,42) = 13.9) and in heart rate (F = 22.6), systolic (F = 26.4) and diastolic blood pressure (F = 12.8) and pupil diameter (F = 6.5) (df 3,42); none of these differed between the groups.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2.2 Visual analog scales and Fig. 1 legend (p. 32); 3.2.5 Physiological measures (p. 33)
key_findings.note: Dose order in this session was fixed and ascending (0, 12.5, 25, 50 mg/70 kg, 1 h apart). For pupil diameter F(3,42) = 6.5 corresponds to p of about 0.001, not below 0.0001 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: The dependence group reported more desire for cocaine before any dose (t[14] = 2.43, p = 0.045) and throughout the dose-response session (group F(1,14) = 6.7, p = 0.022; group by time F(12,168) = 2.3, p = 0.009), with no dose effect; the abuse group started at zero and its desire rose with dose and fell by 45 min.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2.1 Baseline measures; 3.2.2 Visual analog scales; Fig. 1

key_findings.finding: Main effects of group on the adjective checklists: the abuse group was higher on subject-rated suspicious (F = 7.9) and on observer-rated moody (F(1,14) = 4.98, p = 0.043), difficulty concentrating (F = 5.9, p = 0.029), fidgety (F = 5.21, p = 0.039), drug effect (F(1,14) = 4.7) and edgy or irritable (F = 12.2); the dependence group was higher on crave cocaine (F = 6.0) and sweating (F = 7.1). In the editors' reading of Fig. 2, all peak observer means are below 1.5 on the 0 to 4 scale.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2.3 Adjective checklists, 2nd paragraph (p. 33); Fig. 2 (p. 33); 3.2.1 Baseline measures (p. 32)
key_findings.note: Before any dose the abuse group was already rated higher on edgy or irritable (t(14) = -2.65 for CocDep lower, p = 0.033), and in Fig. 2 its means are higher after placebo; no group by dose interaction is reported for these items.

key_findings.finding: Street value given to the doses: group by dose interaction F(3,42) = 5.1, p = 0.005; at 50 mg/70 kg the means were $10.88 (abuse group) and $30.38 (dependence group).

Relapse Choice Procedure (seven choices between the dose and money): the dependence group chose more injections (group F(1,14) = 5.27, p = 0.038; dose F(2,28) = 3.4, p = 0.049), about twice as many at both active doses, with post hoc differences significant at 25 mg/70 kg; money earned fell with dose (F(2,28) = 3.69, p = 0.038), group p = 0.055. The abuse group never chose placebo over money; half of the dependence group chose placebo two or more times.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3.1 Relapse Procedure (p. 33); Fig. 3 and legend (p. 34)
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of the individual points in Fig. 3: mean injections, abuse vs dependence group, 0 vs 1.6 at placebo, 1.5 vs 3.75 at 12.5 mg/70 kg, 2.75 vs about 5.4 at 25 mg/70 kg.

key_findings.finding: Progressive Ratio Procedure: ratios completed rose with dose (F(2,28) = 8.43, p = 0.001); the group difference was not significant (p = 0.056). Three people in the abuse group took no active cocaine in either procedure; one further person in the abuse group and two in the dependence group took none in one procedure.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3.2 Progressive Ratio Procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 33); Fig. 4 and legend (p. 34)
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Fig. 4: ratios completed, abuse vs dependence group, 0 vs 0.25, 2.0 vs about 4.9 and 3.25 vs 6.0 at 0, 12.5 and 25 mg/70 kg. The printed F(1,14) = 3.92 corresponds to p of about 0.068 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Cocaine taken in the two procedures, collapsed across doses, correlated strongly (Spearman rho = 0.76, p < 0.001).

Multiple-Choice Procedure: crossover values (the money value at which money was first preferred) rose with dose (F(2,28) = 6.3, p = 0.006) and were higher in the dependence group (F(1,14) = 4.9, p = 0.044).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.4 Multiple-Choice Procedure; Fig. 5 and legend
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Fig. 5 bars: about $1.2 vs $1.1 at placebo, $1.1 vs $5.6 at 12.5 mg/70 kg and $4.6 vs $9.6 at 25 mg/70 kg (abuse vs dependence group).

key_findings.finding: No group differences on the Barratt scale (64.6 vs 64.8), Eysenck impulsiveness (7.3 vs 8.0), Zuckerman total (18.5 vs 18.9) or any NEO subscale; overall gambling-task choice did not differ, although the dependence group chose fewer disadvantageous cards in two later blocks (trials 21-40 and 81-100, p < 0.05) and ended with play-money winnings of $415.63 against a loss of $387.50 in the abuse group.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 34, means and SEM); Results › 3.5 Trait and impulsivity measures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 34-35); Fig. 6 (p. 35)

key_findings.finding: The authors interpret the abuse group's ratings as possible greater sensitivity to cocaine's unpleasant effects, or tolerance to these effects in the dependence group, and suggest a protective mechanism against escalation.

reporting_issues.issue: The Fig. 1 legend places the abuse group in the right panels and the dependence group in the left, while the panel titles and the text (3.2.2) place the abuse group on the left.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader following the legend would swap the groups; the panel titles and text agree with each other and are taken as correct.

reporting_issues.issue: The Fig. 6 legend calls the white bars the dependent group and the grey bars the non-dependent group, while the key inside the figure and the text make white the abuse group.
reporting_issues.consequence: Same kind of legend error as Fig. 1; the key and text agree and are taken as correct.

reporting_issues.issue: The two baseline t-tests are printed with df = 14, but their p-values correspond to about 7 df: t = 2.43 gives p = 0.029 with 14 df and 0.045 with 7; t = -2.65 gives p = 0.019 with 14 df and 0.033 with 7 (editors' calculation). This fits an unequal-variance test when every abuse-group baseline rating of desire was zero (as the text says).
reporting_issues.consequence: The df are misreported; the conclusions do not change.

reporting_issues.issue: For the progressive-ratio group effect the text and the Fig. 4 legend give F(1,14) = 3.92 with p = 0.056, but F = 3.92 on 1 and 14 df gives p of about 0.068 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the F or the p is misprinted; the effect is not significant either way, yet the Discussion treats the procedures as showing the same group difference.

reporting_issues.issue: Inclusion criteria against Table 1: the abuse group had to use cocaine no more than twice a week (about 8.6 days in 30), but two of its members report 9 and 10 days in the past 30; the dependence group had to use 6 or more days a week (about 25.7 days in 30), but one member reports 20 days.
reporting_issues.consequence: The criteria refer to the 2 months before admission and the table to the past 30 days, so this may reflect different windows; the groups are less sharply separated than the criteria say.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods list six analogue items including bad effects and not high; the Results report high and never report bad effects.
reporting_issues.consequence: The one self-rated measure of unpleasant effects is missing from a paper that concludes the abuse group was more sensitive to unpleasant effects.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives mean age at first use as 23.5 in the abuse group; age minus years since first use in Table 1 gives 23.25 (21.0 in the dependence group, as printed) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; age at first use may have been asked separately.

reporting_issues.issue: The x-axis of Fig. 2 labels the third dose 25.5 mg/70 kg; the dose given was 25 mg/70 kg.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; no effect on the data.

reporting_issues.issue: Several group effects are reported only as F values without df or p (suspicious 7.9, crave cocaine 6.0, sweating 7.1, edgy or irritable 12.2), and the Discussion says intake was reliably but not significantly higher in the Progressive Ratio Procedure than in the Relapse Choice Procedure without any test.
reporting_issues.consequence: These results cannot be checked; the procedure comparison is unsupported.
